page: Alibaba Cloud ecs.r6.2xlarge is a memory-optimized virtual machine instance running on the KVM hypervisor. It is powered by an x86_64 Intel Xeon Platinum 8269CY processor clocked at 2.5 GHz. The instance is provisioned with 8 dedicated vCPUs mapped across 4 physical cores with 2 threads per core, alongside 35 MB of shared L3 cache and support for AVX-512 vector instructions. Memory allocation stands at 64.0 GB of RAM, yielding an 8:1 memory-to-vCPU ratio of 8.0 GB per vCPU. The instance contains no bundled local storage and includes no discrete GPU accelerators. Network connectivity is rated at a baseline bandwidth of 2 Gbps without complimentary public IPv4 addresses.

Benchmark evaluations reveal solid memory-centric throughput paired with moderate compute capacity. Memory bandwidth benchmarks reach 49.43 GB/sec for uncached 256MB reads and 37.84 GB/sec for uncached writes, placing the instance in the middle 50% tier. Redis SET operations perform reliably at 6.84 million operations per second, supported by an average PassMark memory score of 2313.37. Single-threaded compute tests, including Geekbench single-core (1150.0) and stress-ng single-core (1311.09), fall into the bottom 25% bracket, reflecting conservative baseline clock frequencies. However, multi-core tasks scale effectively, with Geekbench multi-core hitting 4380.0 and stress-ng multi-core reaching 6983.38.

The primary architectural tradeoff lies in the balance between high RAM density and modest single-thread speed. Cost efficiency is optimized for environments where application throughput depends heavily on working-set memory capacity rather than raw compute cycles. Because local storage is absent, all persistent storage requirements must rely on external network-attached volumes.

Alibaba Cloud ecs.r6.2xlarge is best suited for memory-intensive workloads that fit into its 64 GB footprint. Recommended production use cases include in-memory databases such as Redis or Memcached, transactional relational databases, intermediate caching layers, batch ETL processing, and enterprise application backends that do not demand extreme per-core compute performance.
